result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.global_reaching_centrality()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Measure how hierarchical a network is with global reaching centrality. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L30303-L30366){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.global_reaching_centrality( weighted=None, normalized=True, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Global reaching centrality](/assets/graphs/global-reaching-centrality.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left, a five-node out-tree, each node badged with the share of other nodes it reaches: A 1, B 0.5, and the leaves 0. Averaging each node's gap to the top value gives (0 + 0.5 + 1 + 1 + 1) / 4 = 0.875, a strong hierarchy. Right, in a directed 4-cycle every node reaches all others, there is no gap, and the score is 0.0." width="100%"} Global reaching centrality (Mones, Vicsek & Vicsek, 2012) compares every node's local reaching centrality (see `local_reaching_centrality()`) with the highest one: `GRC = Σ (C_max - C(v)) / (n - 1)`. A strict hierarchy, where one node reaches everything and others reach little, scores near `1`; a network where everyone reaches about as much as everyone else (a cycle, a complete graph) scores near `0`. It is a single-number test of whether a directed network is organized top-down, used for organizational charts, food webs, citation and dominance networks. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Whether to use edge weights. If `None` (default), follows the graph. [normalized]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : With weights, normalize local reaching centrality by the mean edge weight. Default is `True`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The global reaching centrality. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph has fewer than two nodes or no edges, or a weight is not positive. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} An out-tree is strongly hierarchical; a directed cycle is not hierarchical at all: ::: {#e11c777c .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec tree = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_nodes(["r", "a", "b", "c"]) tree.add_edges([("r", "a"), ("r", "b"), ("a", "c")]) cycle = ec.Graph(directed=True).add_nodes(["a", "b", "c", "d"]) cycle.add_edges([("a", "b"), ("b", "c"), ("c", "d"), ("d", "a")]) round(tree.global_reaching_centrality(), 3), cycle.global_reaching_centrality() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (0.889, 0.0) ``` ::: :::
